source.title: Monet: Mixture of Monosemantic Experts for Transformers
source.authors: Jungwoo Park; Youngjin Ahn; Kee-Eung Kim; Jaewoo Kang

record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses polysemanticity and reports results about its own learned experts, not neuron-pole job shares or the explanation tests named in the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper's interpretability evidence concerns MONET experts rather than ordinary model neurons or neuron poles. It gives qualitative expert examples and self-generated descriptions, but no quantitative share of units with one or multiple jobs. Its expert-removal and toxicity results concern knowledge unlearning and behavior changes, not direct tests of the claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study trains a new MoE architecture (MONET) and shows qualitative examples of specialized routed experts. It does not audit ordinary neurons or neuron poles, give one-job/two-job shares, analyse InceptionV1, build neuron attribution graphs, or score explanations by predicting held-out activations. Its claim that architecture yields monosemantic experts is close to V4. But it reports no share of interpretable units under different tools or architectures, so V4 is not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that MONET's 262,144 experts per layer enable fine-grained, monosemantic specialization and that knowledge can be unlearned across domains, languages and toxicity without degrading general performance. They state that the self-explained experts are shown only qualitatively.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains a new mixture-of-experts architecture with decomposed, routed experts; it does not audit neuron poles or test neuron explanations on held-out activations.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper varies architecture decomposition, model scale, and routing-group setup, but does not report how these choices change a quantitative neuron interpretability share.

fits_no_version.finding: Qualitative examples of MONET experts specialized on concepts (chemical compounds, U.S. states, Bay Area vs Bayesian, string types, colours) in text, code and vision-language variants, plus self-generated expert descriptions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Routed experts in a 262K-expert MoE can show recognizable single-concept specialization in selected examples (no quantified share).

fits_no_version.finding: Under a routing-skew criterion, LLaMA 1.3B has on average 6% of MLP neurons specialized per MMLU domain vs 2.2% of MONET experts. OLMoE had no experts meeting the criterion. The authors read this as feature entanglement or polysemanticity in the baselines (Section 5.1).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Domain-specialization rates of dense-MLP neurons and coarse MoE experts, measured by activation skew, indicate entanglement relative to fine-grained experts.

record.problems: The expert-specialization examples are qualitative. The paper explicitly says quantitative evaluation of automated interpretation remains open. These results do not establish neuron-pole job shares or held-out explanation accuracy.
record.rows_left_out: Domain-specific and programming-language expert deletion and toxic-expert purging results are not included: their reported outcomes concern knowledge unlearning, benchmark performance, or toxicity changes, rather than neuron-pole interpretability or explanation accuracy (Sections 5.1–5.3; Tables 3–5, 11, and 15).

untested.parts: No Qwen3-32B neuron-pole audit or job-share percentages.
No neuron-pole job shares in other dense or MoE models at any scale. The OLMoE and LLaMA results are domain-routing skew for unlearning, not interpretability shares.
No InceptionV1 or classic polysemantic-neuron reanalysis; no pose or recursive-generalization test.
No measured share of interpretable units as a function of architecture or tools. MONET's monosemanticity is shown only by selected qualitative examples.
No attribution graphs or circuit explanations from neurons.
No test of activating-example explanations against where units fire.
No simulation-based scoring. The authors say quantitative evaluation of automated interpretation remains open.

record.verdict_notes: R4's numbers_found value '3/3' has no clear meaning and should be cleared. The unlearning and toxicity results are correctly left out as off-claim. The LLaMA 6% vs MONET 2.2% specialization figure could be added as a non-version row if the phenomenon file wants baseline-neuron context.

versions.untested_parts: No Qwen3-32B audit, neuron-pole count, or one-job/two-job/ununderstood share.
No comparable neuron-pole shares across dense and MoE models or at trillion-parameter scale; MONET's qualitative expert examples do not measure the claimed shares.
No InceptionV1 cat-and-car analysis or test of pose, recursive generalization, or superposition.
No test of the proposed causes of messy late-layer neurons or estimates of interpretable-neuron shares for InceptionV1-sized vision models.
No attribution graphs or test of whether neuron-based graphs explain behavior without a replacement model.
No test of explanations against activations withheld from explanation construction.
The paper says quantitative evaluation of automated interpretation remains open; it does not score explanations by predicting activations on new text.

rows.subject: MONET-1.4B
rows.operation_detail: Examined expert routing scores and activated tokens in qualitative examples.

conditions.value: chemical compounds, U.S. states, Bay-area geography, and Bayesian-related text

rows.measure: Qualitative correspondence between expert routing and activated-token contexts.
rows.value: The paper presents experts associated with chemical compounds and U.S. states, and two different experts associated with geographical “Bay” and Bayesian contexts.
rows.note: These are expert examples, not neuron-pole job classifications or a quantified interpretability rate.

rows.subject: MONET-4.1B
rows.operation_detail: Examined expert routing scores and activated tokens in qualitative examples.
rows.measure: Qualitative correspondence between expert routing and activated-token contexts.
rows.value: The paper presents an expert whose examples are associated with electromagnetism and physicists in that field.

rows.subject: CODE MONET-1.4B
rows.operation_detail: Examined expert routing scores and activated code tokens.
rows.measure: Qualitative correspondence between expert routing and code-token contexts.
rows.value: The paper presents an expert that consistently maps string-related knowledge across programming languages.
rows.note: This reports an expert-level example, not a neuron share.

rows.subject: MONET-1.4B CHAT
rows.operation_detail: Prompted the model to describe experts using averaged token embeddings activated to each target expert.

conditions.value: Question asking for the meaning of a word represented by the averaged activated token embeddings

rows.value: The model generated descriptions including “Cartilage” for Expert 232,717 and “Expertise” for Expert 51; the paper states that these demonstrations are qualitative.
rows.note: No quantitative scoring or held-out activation prediction is reported.

rows.subject: VISION MONET-1.4B
rows.operation_detail: Examined text and image examples routed to multimodal experts.

conditions.value: CC3M image examples and associated text

rows.measure: Qualitative correspondence between expert routing and multimodal concepts.
rows.value: The paper reports examples of different experts specializing in concepts such as Green versus Purple, Black versus Sunlight, and Aviation versus Body of Water.
rows.note: This is qualitative evidence about MONET experts, not ordinary neurons or neuron-pole shares.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
